title: With This Nation the World Can Be Conquered
paragraphs: One day the king changed his clothes and went out into the city to observe how the people lived. To learn about the quality of the goods, the prices, and the mood of the shopkeepers, he began to inspect the city markets.
The king entered the first shop at the head of the street. Greeting them, he said:
— Give me half a batman of oil, half a batman of honey, and a little cheese.

The shopkeeper welcomed the customer with a smile, returned the greeting courteously, and gladly weighed out half a batman of oil. As he handed over the oil, not knowing that the man before him was the king, he addressed him thus:

— My lord, if you wish, I can give you the honey and cheese as well. But by selling this oil I have already made my siftah—the first sale of the day. If you would buy your other needs from my neighbor across the way, who has not yet made his first sale, I would be most pleased.
Glad at heart, the king paid for the oil and crossed to the shop opposite. There too he asked for half a batman of honey and some cheese. After weighing the honey, the elderly shopkeeper said:
— Thank God, thanks to you we have made our first sale today as well. But I ask this of you: take the cheese not from me, but from the shop next door. He has not yet made his first sale.
Deeply moved by what he had seen, the king went to the neighboring shop, completed his purchases, and then said:
— When a nation possesses such high morals, the whole world can be conquered, — and he left the market happy and content.
True strength lies not in weapons, but in the honesty and uprightness of the people. The real victory is not the taking of land, but the conquest of hearts.

title: The Story of the Bedouin Whose Camel Was Stolen
paragraphs: A Bedouin traveling through the desert with his camel came upon a man barely able to stand, his lips cracked with thirst. The man begged the Bedouin for water to drink. The Bedouin dismounted and gave him water. The man drank, then suddenly shoved the Bedouin aside, mounted the camel, and made to flee.
When the Bedouin saw that he could do nothing to save his camel, he called after the thief:
— So be it—take the camel; it is yours. But never tell this story to anyone.
Astonished by the Bedouin's strange request, the thief paused for a moment, looked back, and asked the reason.
— If you tell it, the story will spread everywhere, and no one will ever again help a needy person they meet, — the Bedouin answered.
Sometimes concealing one's own loss serves to protect others' faith in goodness. A single evil tale can close a thousand doors of kindness.

title: The Woman Whose House Was Robbed
paragraphs: In ancient times an old woman's house in a certain city was robbed. Distraught, she came before the king to complain. The king listened and asked angrily: "And why did you sleep so deeply that you did not even notice a thief enter your house?" The woman replied: "Long live the Shah—we thought that you were awake, and so we slept at ease in our homes."
The people's peace rests on their trust in the state. If people believe their ruler is awake, they sleep at ease in their own homes.

title: The Just Verdict of the Frankfurt Judge
paragraphs: This incident was recorded in the city of Frankfurt in 1506. A merchant lost on the road a purse containing eight hundred gulden. A carpenter who happened to pass that way found the purse. Being a man of deep piety, he told no one of his find and reasoned that it was impossible not to notice the loss of so much money—therefore the owner would surely come searching.

One day the carpenter came to church to worship. After the service the priest announced to the congregation that a merchant who had come to Frankfurt had lost eight hundred gulden and promised a reward of one hundred gulden to whoever found and returned them.
Hearing this, the carpenter took the money he had found, came to the church, and handed the purse to the priest.

The merchant was told that his money had been found; he came to the church, took the purse, yet refused to pay the carpenter the promised hundred gulden—giving him only five. The carpenter asked the merchant to keep his word. The greedy merchant, to avoid paying the hundred gulden, claimed that his purse had held nine hundred, not eight hundred, and that the carpenter had taken money from it. The priest entered the dispute in the carpenter's defense, saying he knew him for an honest man who would do no such thing. The argument grew heated. The priest took the merchant and the carpenter before the city court.

The trial began. The judge required the merchant to place his hand upon the Bible and swear that he had lost nine hundred gulden. Without hesitation the merchant laid his hand on the Bible and swore. The judge then asked the carpenter to swear that he had found eight hundred gulden. The carpenter too pressed his hand upon the Bible and swore.
Everyone waited impatiently for the judge's decision. The judge said that everything was as clear as day and announced his ruling thus:

— The carpenter found eight hundred gulden, and the merchant lost nine hundred. Therefore the money the carpenter found is not the merchant's. Since no owner has been found, these eight hundred gulden are awarded to the carpenter. As for the merchant, he may continue to search for the nine hundred gulden he lost.
Greed springs its own trap. The miser who denies what is right ends as the victim of his own lie; justice stands with the one who is in the right.

title: Nazim Hikmet in Bursa Prison
paragraphs: The Turkish poet Nazim Hikmet was serving his sentence in Bursa Prison. One day an inspector from the Ministry of Justice came to examine the prison. He asked the warden to summon Nazim Hikmet—he wished to meet him.

They called Nazim. He entered the room… A brief conversation took place between them. But the ministry official did not invite the poet to sit. After the talk he said, "You may go." As Nazim Hikmet was leaving through the doorway, he turned back and asked the inspector:
— Do you know Omar Khayyam?
— Of course. How could one not know him?
— And can you tell me who the shah was in Omar Khayyam's time?
The inspector was astonished by this unexpected question and could not answer.
Nazim Hikmet said:
— You see—you remembered the artist, but not the shah. A time will come when neither the minister of justice nor you will be remembered. But my name will always be remembered.
With that he went out. The inspector understood his mistake. Though he called after him, the poet did not turn back…
With the passage of time, those who hold office are forgotten; those who create true value remain in memory. Rank is fleeting; deeds endure.

title: The Bell to Hang on the Cat's Neck
paragraphs: A band of mice gathered to seek a way of escaping a cat that had become the bane of their lives.
Many ideas were put forward, but none was accepted. At last a young mouse proposed hanging a bell around the cat's neck.

The essence of the plan was this: as the cat with a bell around its neck drew near, the mice would hear the ringing and flee, and so save their lives. The proposal was greeted by all the mice with great enthusiasm and applause.
At that moment an old mouse who had been watching in silence from a corner spoke up:
— This is a very clever proposal, and if it were carried out I have no doubt it would succeed. But one question troubles me: tell me, then—who will hang the bell around the cat's neck?
It is easy to make a plan and hard to carry it out. Even the brightest idea is worthless if it is never put into practice.

title: The Skins of the Lambs
paragraphs: "Better to shear the rams than to flay the lambs."
This saying is linked with the name of Azmzadeh Asad Pasha, who in Ottoman times was governor of the province of Damascus. The story goes as follows:

One day Asad Pasha's treasury ran empty, and he fell into great distress. His advisers recommended, as a way to refill the treasury, that he levy an extra tax on the weavers of Damascus. Listening to the advice, Asad Pasha asked: "If we impose such a tax, how much revenue would we gain?"
— We would take fifty or sixty purses of gold, — they said.
Asad Pasha objected: "These people already scrape by with difficulty. How are they to pay this tax?" The advisers tried to persuade him: "They will sell the gold and jewels in their houses, Pasha."
Asad Pasha said: "I shall obtain this sum by a better means."
The advisers fell silent.
The next day the Pasha sent an invitation to the mufti and proposed a secret meeting at night. That night the mufti came to visit the Pasha. The Pasha said:

— Efendi Mufti! According to information we have obtained, in your private life you act contrary to the Sharia and secretly drink liquor at home. I must report this state of affairs to Istanbul. But I thought I should warn you first.

Hearing this, the mufti began to plead with the Pasha. To keep him from sending word to Istanbul, he offered a thousand mecidiye. The Pasha refused. The mufti offered twice as much. The Pasha refused again. At last they agreed on six thousand mecidiye.
The next day Asad Pasha invited the qadi and said to him: "Efendi Qadi, from reliable sources we have learned that you take bribes and use your office for private gain."

This time the qadi began to plead with the Pasha. Like the mufti, he bargained with Asad Pasha: "Ah, my lord, do not remove me from my post, or I shall be disgraced among the people." They agreed with the qadi as well on six thousand mecidiye.
Then Asad Pasha invited, one by one, the treasurer, the chief of security, the merchants, and the wealthy to meet with him.

At the end of this operation Asad Pasha had gathered fully two hundred purses of mecidiye gold. Then he summoned his advisers and asked: "Have you heard that I levied a tax on the people of Damascus?" "No, we have not heard," they said.
The Pasha said: "Though I levied no tax, I have gathered not fifty but two hundred purses of mecidiye gold."
— How did you do it, Pasha?
The Pasha answered: "Better to shear the rams than to flay the lambs."
It is more just to take the unjust gains of the powerful than to strip the poor. The burden should be laid not on the weak, but on the strong.

title: Homeland and Land
paragraphs: Add water to earth and it becomes mud; add blood and it becomes a homeland.
What turns land into a homeland is the blood shed for its sake. A homeland is not merely a place—it is a sacred trust for which sacrifice is made.

title: Why Injustice When There Is Justice
paragraphs: Haji Bektash Veli:
When there is love, why hatred,
When there is peace, why war,
When there is brotherhood, why strife,
When there is friendship, why enmity,
When there is forbearance, why intolerance,
When there is freedom, why captivity,
When there is justice, why injustice?
When love, peace, brotherhood, and justice are possible, to choose hatred, quarrel, and injustice is a person's own sin.

title: Sharing Justice
paragraphs: Either let no one weep,
or let those who always laugh laugh no more;
either let no one be plagued by this disease called money,
or let the nation that has money learn to share;
either let no one speak of the one they love,
or let them give the true praise of real love;
either let these feast days never be lived,
or let no one go without meat on the feast.
When joy, and bread, and love are shared, humanity is born. Where one side laughs and the other weeps, there is no justice.
